title: What's running — going up
brief: This is a phone-first page that answers one question in about a second: is anything running right now? In motion means a task an agent is working on at this moment, which is the building and verifying statuses and nothing else. On the corpus today that is four tasks and it is frequently zero, so the nearly-empty page is the state this design lives in most of the time and the empty state is a primary design rather than an edge case handled last. Emptiness is information and must read as deliberate rather than as a page that failed to load. It is built for a phone held in one hand and read at a glance, so the layout starts at roughly three hundred and seventy pixels wide and grows from there. Touch targets are generous, nothing depends on hover and nothing depends on a pointer. The corpus is live over an SSE feed. Dark is the sole colour mode and status colour is reserved for state, never decoration. This round builds directly on a winning approach that gave the same content two scales, a grid of every runner at once and a single full-screen card, with one control moving between them. The grid is the landing state because the question is plural, four cells answer it in one frame with no gesture, and a cell is a nameplate rather than a shrunken card, carrying a status rule and word, an id, a project, a release, an elapsed time and a phase, but deliberately no title, because at that size a title is a clipped promise. Identity survives the transition in both directions: the current cell is marked and takes focus on the way out, and the deck positions instantly rather than smoothly on the way back in, because a smooth scroll replays the intervening cards and reads as the page losing your place. That approach is kept and every approach in this round keeps it. What is new is that the reader now wants to go up. From the task being read they want to reach its release and its project, following the hierarchy the corpus already has, where a task sits in a release and a release sits in a project. This must be very simple. It is navigation upward from where the reader already stands rather than a browser of the whole corpus, and it is not a filter and not a context switcher. The earlier brief forbade a second level entirely and that constraint is now deliberately relaxed for the upward move alone, which means every approach must be honest about what the relaxation costs a page whose whole argument was that it had no second level. The downward direction is unchanged: there is still no search, no board, no backlog, and anything that is not building or verifying still has no place in the running view.

approaches.title: The third scale
approaches.direction: Extends the winning approach's own zoom metaphor upward so that the scales run from one task card out to the grid and further out to the release and the project, testing whether the control that already moves between two scales can simply keep going and make the hierarchy a continuation rather than a new mechanism.
deviations: The seeded shell is replaced: no Footer, and PageSection, Container and PageHeader are not used. The page is a single flex column exactly one viewport tall. Why: A horizontal pager inside a vertically scrolling document is the known misery, so the document is made exactly one screen tall and the deck track is the only horizontal scroller. Inherited unchanged from the approach this round builds on.

ToggleGroup is not used at all. The scale control is two bare <button> elements plus a four-tick position strip. review_markup reports both buttons as raw-element. Why: The winning approach used ToggleGroup for two positions and had to :global into it to lift the 34px segments to 44px. At four rungs it is not salvageable: it still emits no aria-pressed, and four segments on a 370px phone are 84px each, which cannot hold a release slug. Button was equally wrong — it is a pill with one centred label, and a rung is a direction word over a slug. Reported, not fixed.

The ladder button prints the destination name but not its kind. Only the aria-label says "the release prototype-loop-v1". Why: Measured at 370px: each half of the control is 165px, and RELEASE · WIDER wrapped onto two lines and pushed prototype-loop-v1 into an ellipsis. Between naming the kind and naming the place, the place is the one the reader cannot infer from the destination screen it leads to.

Literal font-size ceilings in three clamps: 1.75rem on the page heading and the release slug, 2.125rem on the project slug. Why: The public type scale stops at --text-lead (1.25rem), which is a caption size on a panel that owns the screen. The floor is the token; no token exists that would have prevented the ceiling.

The release title and the project rung release titles use -webkit-line-clamp with the unprefixed line-clamp beside it. Why: There is no line-clamp utility in the library and no token for it. At 370px an unclamped release title took three lines and pushed the marked roster entry off the screen, which is the one thing on that rung that has to be visible on arrival.

padding-bottom on the page is calc(var(--space-7) + var(--space-5)) rather than var(--space-4). Why: Clears the prototyping harness floating pager, which is fixed to the bottom of every /dev page and would otherwise cover the ladder. A production page would carry var(--space-4) here like every other edge.

The release rung renders tasks that are not building or verifying — done, pending, triaged, blocked. Why: This is the one place the brief has been read as permitting non-running work, and it is deliberate. A release showing only its runners is the grid filtered by project, which the reader already had, so the rung would carry no information. It is contained: nothing on that rung is interactive, so no non-running task can be opened and the running view itself is unchanged.

The release and project rungs are read-only. Their entries are neither links nor buttons, and the roster area is a scroll container. Why: Making an ancestor entry tappable would turn the ladder into a browser of the corpus, which the relaxation did not license, and would break the guarantee that coming down lands on the task you left. The scroll container is safe here because no horizontal gesture lives at those rungs, so it cannot eat one.

Pill is used for release tags with fill="outline" and tint="var(--text-muted)" rather than its canonical warm treatment. Why: Pill canonically tints toward --burnt-sunset, which sits beside --amber. On a page where amber means building, a decorative tag in a neighbouring hue is exactly the decoration the brief forbids.

approaches.title: The standing line
approaches.direction: Prints the project, the release and the task as one persistent line on the card with every segment reachable, so the reader's position in the hierarchy is always visible and every ancestor is always one tap, testing whether the plainest and most conventional answer is also the best one here.
deviations: The library DOES have a Breadcrumb and it is not used. The brief said there was none; find_components returned it as live, in navigation. It is built out of <a href>, and going up here is a change of view inside one prototype route rather than a document fetch, so an href would be a claim about a URL that does not exist. Its segments are also text with no height — roughly 20px — against a 44px floor, and it sets font-size 0.875rem and font-weight 500 as literals with hover as its only affordance. A local StandingLine replaces it. The finding is not that the library lacks a breadcrumb but that its breadcrumb is a document-navigation atom and this page needs an application one.

The seeded shell is stripped, carried over from the winning approach: no Footer, no PageSection, no PageHeader, no Container. The page is exactly one screen tall so that the deck's horizontal swipe is not fighting a vertically scrolling document, and the h1 is the answer to the page's question rather than a title above it.

ScaleControl reaches into ToggleGroup's own class names to raise its segments from 34px to 44px. The atom pins 44px to its shell, not its segments, and emits no aria-pressed on the active option; the second is not fixable from outside, so the page's live readout carries the announcement instead. Unchanged from the winning approach and re-reported here.

Three bare <button> elements — the standing line's segments, the release view's task rows, the project view's release rows — all flagged by review_markup as raw-element. Button is a pill with fixed padding and a centred label; a segment inside a breadcrumb and a two- or three-line full-width row are neither. Named in the report as components the library does not have.

review_markup's raw-value fix is declined in two places: it reports text-underline-offset: 3px as 'exactly --frost-2' and offers to substitute it. --frost-2 is an elevation/blur token; the rule matches by value and cannot see category. Taking the fix would tie an underline offset to a shadow scale.

The relaxation of 'no second level' is spent in one direction only, and it costs the page its cleanest rule. The release view renders every ledger status, not just building and verifying, because a release contains everything and most of it is not running. Status colour is still spent on those two alone — a done task is a word in the muted colour — but the claim that the page never shows you anything that is not in motion now holds for the running view rather than for the page.

The literal type ceilings (2.125rem, 1.75rem) survive from the winning approach and are joined by two more in the upward views. The public scale stops at --text-lead (1.25rem), which is a caption size on a panel that owns the screen. The clamp floor is a token every time; the ceiling cannot be. review_markup's raw-value rule is silent on all of them, which is a good illustration of its documented limit: silence from it is not a clean bill.

approaches.title: Pushed
approaches.direction: Treats an ancestor as a destination pushed onto a stack, so tapping a release opens it as a full screen with a way back, testing the phone-native pattern of depth as a stack against a page that until now has deliberately had no depth at all.
deviations: BREACH of 'anything that is not building or verifying still has no place in the running view': a release screen renders every task in the release, including done, blocked, pending, triaged, wontfix and duplicate, grouped by integer phase. A five-task release rendered as its one building task is a lie about the release, told to protect a rule that was written about the running view. The rule is kept where it was written — the grid and the deck still cannot express a non-running status, and RunningStatus is a narrower type than TaskStatus so the compiler enforces it — and relaxed only on a screen the reader reached by deciding to leave.

Status colour extended from the reserved pair to all eight ledger labels, because a release screen cannot be honest with two. Amber and blush still mean building and verifying and nothing else; triaged takes --sky-blue, done --olive-green, blocked --fire-engine-red, and pending, wontfix and duplicate share --text-muted rather than each being given a colour it has not earned. Every mark carries its word, and only the two motion statuses breathe — movement is reserved the same way colour is.

The whole navigation stack lives in the LOCATION HASH rather than the path. The prototyping harness routes on location.pathname (src/dev/App.svelte) and would unmount the page the moment a push moved the path; the query already carries ?empty and ?live and a navigation mechanism that clobbers the page's own state parameters is a bug waiting for the first reload. A production page would push a real path. The interaction under test — pushState, popstate, the phone's own back — is identical either way.

The pushed screens are rendered as siblings of PageFrame rather than inside it. PageFrame's column sets position: relative and z-index: var(--z-raised), which makes the whole shell including the Header one stacking context, so a fixed screen rendered inside it can never rise above the Header at --z-widget. Measured at 370px before the change: the site wordmark intercepted every click aimed at the back control, which is the one control a pushed screen must have. Reported as a library finding — a full-screen push has nowhere legal to stand inside PageFrame.

--filter-control-height is abandoned as the touch-target floor and replaced with --space-7 in four places (both card destinations, the release screen's project destination, the project screen's release rows, and ScaleControl's segments). Measured: the token is 2.75rem on a phone but 2.25rem from 640px up, so the controls came out 41px at 1280px — under the 44px minimum at exactly the width where a touchscreen laptop reads this page. --space-7 is 48px at every width. The ScaleControl case is inherited from the winning approach and was under the floor there too.

Off-screen deck slots are now inert. The approach this builds on left them exposed on purpose, because the cards held no controls and four cards read end to end beat one card plus a gesture. Every card now carries two destination buttons, so eight off-screen buttons sat in the tab order and a reader tabbing off card one landed on card three's release. The cost is that the deck is one card at a time for assistive technology as well now. This is the relaxation billing the deck.

Two bare <button> elements on the card, one on the release screen and one per row on the project screen, all reported by review_markup as raw-element. A destination is a three-column row — rank, name, chevron — that fills the width and holds a 48px target; Button is a centred pill with a fixed height and its own padding. Named in the report as the single component the library does not have and this approach needs four times.

BackLink is not used for the back control. It is required to carry an href, and back here is history.back() rather than a document fetch, so an href would be a claim about a URL that the control does not actually navigate to. Its fixed mode pins below the header, which a full-screen push has covered. The library Button carries the control instead, at its default 3rem height.

Going up exists at card scale only. A grid cell is a nameplate with exactly one action — open this at full size — and a second and third target inside a 158px cell would fight it. The consequence is stated rather than hidden: from the landing state, going up is two taps, and in the empty state, which is the state this page lives in most of the time, there is no way up at all.

Literal font-size ceilings in three clamps: 2.125rem on the card title, 1.75rem on the page heading and on a pushed screen's name. The public type scale stops at --text-lead (1.25rem), which is a caption size for the name of the screen you are standing on. The floor is a token every time; no token exists that would have prevented the ceiling, and raw-value is silent on all three — a good illustration of its documented limit.

The card's internal spacing is tightened from the approach this builds on: gap --space-3 rather than --space-5, padding --space-4 rather than --space-5, and a lower title clamp. Measured at 370x800 before the change, the title printed over the first destination row. Two 48px rows and their gap cost this card 128px of height it used to spend on the title, and that is where the second level is paid for.

Inherited from the winning approach and unchanged: the seeded shell's Footer, PageSection, Container and PageHeader are dropped, because the running view is exactly one screen tall and a footer below the fold would reintroduce the vertical scroll the deck must not fight.

Inherited and unchanged: padding-bottom on the running view and on every pushed screen is calc(var(--space-7) + var(--space-5)) rather than var(--space-4), to clear the prototyping harness's floating pager.

approaches.title: Consulted, not visited
approaches.direction: Brings the release and the project to the reader as a sheet rising over the card rather than sending the reader to them, so the ancestor is consulted without ever leaving the deck, testing whether going up can be done without going anywhere.
deviations: BREACH of 'anything that is not building or verifying still has no place in the running view': the sheet lists every task in the release, including done, blocked, triaged, pending, wontfix and duplicate. A release listing filtered to the two running statuses would report a four-task release as a one-task release, which is a lie about the release told in order to protect a rule about the deck. The rule is kept where it belongs — the deck and the grid still cannot express a non-running status, and the type system says so — and relaxed only inside the sheet.

Status colour extended from the reserved pair to all eight ledger statuses, because the sheet cannot list a release honestly with two. Amber and blush still mean building and verifying and nothing else; triaged takes --sky-blue, done --olive-green, blocked --fire-engine-red, and pending, wontfix and duplicate share --text-muted rather than each being given a colour they do not earn. Every mark carries its word.

Going up exists at card scale only. A second target inside a 158px grid cell would fight the cell's one job, which is to open the card, so the ancestry is reachable from the task being read and not from the grid.

The sheet and its scrim sit at --z-widget rather than --z-overlay. Measured: the site Header is --z-widget (50), so an overlay at 30 left a dialog that was modal to the keyboard and to a screen reader and walked around by a mouse.

Inherited from the winning approach and unchanged: the seeded shell's Footer is dropped, because this page is exactly one screen tall and a footer below the fold reintroduces the vertical scroll the deck must not fight.
Inherited from the winning approach and unchanged: ScaleControl reaches into ToggleGroup's own class names to raise its 34px segments to 44px.

approaches.title: The deck changes hands
approaches.direction: Makes going up refill the deck with the whole of that release or project rather than open a page about it, so the upward move changes what the deck contains instead of where the reader is, and deliberately admits tasks that are not running in order to find out what that costs.
deviations: Tasks that are not building or verifying are rendered on this page. A release deck holds done, blocked, pending, triaged, wontfix and duplicate work alongside the running task; a project deck is mostly finished work. Why: Commissioned by this approach's direction and the single hardest thing about it. Going up refills the deck rather than opening a page, so the set the deck receives is whatever the release or project actually contains, and filtering it back down to running would make the upward move return one card or none — which is not a release. What it cost, measured: eight status colours instead of two; the card's rail stops being a rail above four cards, which is exactly the running set and nothing else; and the grid stops being a glance at seven cells on a 370x667 phone, where sixteen cells scroll to 1172px inside a 321px box. Two devices keep the page from becoming a chart — only building and verifying animate, and every settled status renders at --opacity-tertiary — so the one running cell in a project of sixteen is still the only thing at full strength.

The seeded shell's Footer is dropped and PageSection, Container and PageHeader are not used. The page is a single flex column exactly one viewport tall. Why: A horizontal pager inside a vertically scrolling document is the known misery, so the document is made exactly one screen tall and the deck's own track is the only horizontal scroller. Inherited from the winning approach, which recorded the same deviation.

The card's title is line-clamped — four lines normally, two below a 760px viewport height — where the winning approach let it run. Why: The upward move costs the card a 44px control row and the scope bar costs the page another 44px, and on a 370x667 phone the card's content box is 233px. Measured before the clamp: the identity block was flex-shrunk to zero and the title, the status mark and the id all disappeared behind the progress block, and the 44px up-row rendered underneath it where it was unclickable. The clamp is the honest version of the same shortage — the reader sees a truncation rather than a rendering fault. On a 370x800 phone the four-line clamp never binds.

The card's four counts render label-beside-number on one line rather than stacked, and the progress block's type sizes are one step smaller than the winning approach's. Why: Same shortage, opposite end of the card. The progress block is fixed height by design so the numbers never move between cards, which means every pixel it spends comes straight off the title. Compacting it returned 32px, which is a whole line of title on a short phone.

Inside a release or project deck the tasks are ordered running-first, then by phase and id. The running deck keeps ledger order. Why: A release is mostly finished work, and dropping the reader into a wall of done would bury the one thing this page exists for. Nothing is hidden — the count in the heading is over the whole set — so this is ordering rather than filtering, and it makes 'one running of four' verifiable in the same glance that reads it. It has a cost, seen in the browser: when a task lands over the feed it moves band, so a card slides position under the reader. That is why the reader's place is held as a task id rather than an index.

ToggleGroup's segment height is overridden through :global(.toggle-btn), and the deck rail's icon Buttons are pinned to var(--filter-control-height) through :global(button). Why: ToggleGroup's 44px is the shell around 34px segments, which is under the touch minimum on a page whose whole premise is one-handed use. Button's icon size is a fixed 3rem square; four pixels back from each of two arrows matter on a screen that is exactly full. Both are library defects reported rather than preferences.

A local visually-hidden class is written out on the page's aria-live region. Why: A refill replaces the entire content of the region below the heading, which has to be announced rather than shown, and the library has no visually-hidden utility. Reported as a gap.

UpFromHere, TaskCell and the release plates in NothingRunning are bare <button> elements (raw-element), and the deck's ticks are too. Why: Button is a centred pill sized to its label. A grid nameplate, a half-width two-line plate and a 44px hit area around a 4px bar each require removing Button's padding, height, background and content layout, which would be a Button in name only. All are named plainly in the report as components the library does not have.
